chief_complaint: sudden attacks of rapid pounding heartbeat and dizziness lasting 20 minutes
hpi_details: Presents with a 1-year history of sudden-onset, unprovoked episodes of rapid, regular pounding palpitations in her chest. Attacks start abruptly like a switch being flipped and stop just as suddenly. During episodes, she feels lightheaded, anxious, and notices a strong urge to urinate (polyuria) afterwards. Yesterday's attack lasted 25 minutes while sitting at her office desk. Denies chest pain or loss of consciousness.
ideas: thinks too much coffee and work stress are causing panic attacks
concerns: worried her heart rate is going so fast that her heart will stop beating
expectations: wants a monitor to capture the rhythm and advice on how to stop attacks when they start
social_hx: drinks 3 cups of coffee daily, non-smoker, accountant, goes to gym 3 times/week

available_results.value: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm with retrograde P waves buried in the QRS complexes

clinical_knowledge.topic: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes teaching the patient vagal manoeuvres for acute self-termination of future attacks (modified Valsalva manoeuvre with leg elevation; seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, or a persistent episode), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden attacks of rapid pounding heartbeat and dizziness lasting 20 minutes

Key HPI features: Presents with a 1-year history of sudden-onset, unprovoked episodes of rapid, regular pounding palpitations in her chest. Attacks start abruptly like a switch being flipped and stop just as suddenly. During episodes, she feels lightheaded, anxious, and notices a strong urge to urinate (polyuria) afterwards. Yesterday's attack lasted 25 minutes while sitting at her office desk. Denies chest pain or loss of consciousness.

Objective/Exam findings: During attack: 12-lead ECG shows narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180 bpm with no visible P waves or retrograde P waves buried in QRS. Between attacks: baseline 12-lead ECG completely normal (check for pre-excitation/delta waves of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome). Bloods: thyroid function tests (TSH/T4 to rule out hyperthyroidism), electrolytes, FBC.
Relevant background/PMH: none, healthy young female
Current medications: combined oral contraceptive pill OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Atrial fibrillation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Episodes with chest pain, breathlessness, or collapse.
management_principles: Teach patient vagal manoeuvres for acute self-termination of future attacks (modified Valsalva manoeuvre with leg elevation; seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, or a persistent episode)
Acute hospital protocol if persistent: IV adenosine rapid bolus (6mg -> 12mg -> 12mg) with continuous ECG monitoring
Outpatient referral to cardiac electrophysiology for consideration of curative catheter ablation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients with Supraventricular Tachycardia

reference_soap.subjective: 28F presents with abrupt-onset, abrupt-termination episodes of rapid regular palpitations accompanied by presyncope and post-attack polyuria. Normal baseline health.
reference_soap.objective: During attack: 12-lead ECG shows narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180 bpm with no visible P waves or retrograde P waves buried in QRS. Between attacks: baseline 12-lead ECG completely normal (check for pre-excitation/delta waves of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome). Bloods: thyroid function tests (TSH/T4 to rule out hyperthyroidism), electrolytes, FBC.
reference_soap.assessment: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT) - likely Atrioventricular Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVNRT) or AVRT. DDx: sinus tachycardia from anxiety/caffeine, atrial flutter with 2:1 block, hyperthyroidism, panic attacks.
reference_soap.plan: Teach patient vagal manoeuvres for acute self-termination of future attacks (modified Valsalva manoeuvre with leg elevation; seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, or a persistent episode). Acute hospital protocol if persistent: IV adenosine rapid bolus (6mg -> 12mg -> 12mg) with continuous ECG monitoring. Outpatient referral to cardiac electrophysiology for consideration of curative catheter ablation. Advise caffeine moderation.

learning_objectives: Differentiate paroxysmal SVT from sinus tachycardia based on abrupt onset/termination mechanics and regular rate >150 bpm
Explain the physiological mechanism of post-tachycardia polyuria (atrial stretch releasing Atrial Natriuretic Peptide - ANP)
Instruct the patient on safe and effective execution of the modified Valsalva manoeuvre
Outline the stepped pharmacological termination protocol using rapid IV adenosine boluses

teaching.one_liner: An electrical short-circuit that flips the heart into a fast, regular rhythm — starts and stops abruptly, like a switch.
red_flags: Episodes with chest pain, breathlessness, or collapse

must_ask.say: Does it start and stop suddenly, like flicking a switch?
Is the fast beat regular, and roughly how fast does it feel?
Do you feel a pounding or fullness in your neck during an episode?
Does anything stop it — holding your breath, coughing, splashing cold water?
How often do these attacks happen, and how long do they last?
How much coffee or energy drink do you have in a day?

history.answer: I came to the clinic because I have been having sudden attacks of my heart racing and pounding out of nowhere, and it makes me feel really dizzy.
My heart suddenly beats super fast, like it is fluttering at a crazy speed, but it does not feel like it skips beats.
If I tap it out, it is completely steady and regular, like a tiny jackhammer going very fast.
It starts abruptly like someone flipped an electric switch, and then it suddenly snaps right back to normal when it stops.
I have had these episodes for about a year, happening once or twice a month, and yesterday's attack lasted twenty-five minutes while I was at work.
There is no clear trigger because it can happen while I am just sitting quietly, though it seems more frequent when I have work deadlines.
Nothing specific seems to stop it; I usually just sit down and wait until it suddenly cuts off on its own.
I felt lightheaded and dizzy during the episode yesterday, but I have never actually passed out or blacked out.
No, I do not have chest pain or trouble catching my breath, just the frightening fast heartbeat.
No, I have not been sensitive to heat, sweating excessively, or losing any weight.
I do not feel unusually tired, and I have not had heavy periods or black stools.
No, I do not get throbbing headaches, cold sweats, or pale skin during the attacks, and I do not get shaky when hungry.
I feel very nervous and scared when the racing starts, but I do not hyperventilate and my fingers do not go numb.
No, I have not had a cold, sore throat, or fever recently.
I drink about three cups of coffee every day at the office, but I never drink energy drinks.
No, I do not take cold medicines, nasal sprays, diet pills, or asthma inhalers.
No, I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, a heart condition, or an abnormal heart rhythm.
No, nobody in my family has had sudden unexpected death at a young age or heart rhythm problems.
Yes, while my heart is racing I can actually feel a very prominent pulsing and pounding in my neck and throat.
Yes, every time right after the racing stops, I suddenly have to run to the bathroom to pee a lot.
I have been wondering if all the coffee I drink and my work stress are triggering some kind of panic attacks.
I am terrified that my heart is beating so fast that it might just give out and stop beating.
I would like to get a heart monitor to catch what rhythm this is, and learn how I can stop it when it starts.
I have always been completely healthy with no chronic medical problems.
I have never had surgery and have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take a daily combined birth control pill, and I do not take any herbal supplements or other medications.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I only drink alcohol socially, maybe a glass or two of wine a month.
I work as an accountant, live alone, and go to the gym three times a week.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycle is regular on the pill, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 74 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing young female resting comfortably with no acute distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
No exophthalmos, lid retraction, or lid lag.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules, goiter, or bruits.
No resting or postural tremor noted in outstretched hands.
Internal jugular venous pressure is not elevated, and no cannon a-waves are observed.
Chest wall is non-tender with a normal, non-displaced apical impulse.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Radial pulses are regular, symmetric, and normal in volume at 74 beats per minute.
